validated_results.journal: Annals of oncology : official journal of the European Society for Medical Oncology
validated_results.reason: Pooled Italian case-control analysis of alcohol consumption and incident, histologically confirmed renal cell carcinoma reporting adjusted odds ratios by drinks per day.

extraction.population: Hospital-based incident histologically confirmed RCC cases and controls hospitalised with acute, non-neoplastic conditions

sample_size.excerpt: We investigated the relation using data from two Italian multicentric case-control studies conducted from 1985 to 2004, including a total of 1115 incident, histologically confirmed cases and 2582 controls hospitalised with acute, non-neoplastic conditions.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 1115 + 2582 = 3697

cases.excerpt: We investigated the relation using data from two Italian multicentric case-control studies conducted from 1985 to 2004, including a total of 1115 incident, histologically confirmed cases and 2582 controls hospitalised with acute, non-neoplastic conditions.

effect_size.excerpt: Compared with non-drinkers, the multivariate odds ratios (ORs) of RCC were 0.87 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.73-1.04] for <or=4 drinks per day, 0.76 (95% CI 0.59-0.99) for >4 to <or=8 drinks per day and 0.70 (95% CI 0.50-0.97) for >8 drinks per day of alcoholic beverages, with a significant inverse trend in risk (P value = 0.01).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Compared with non-drinkers, the multivariate odds ratios (ORs) of RCC were 0.87 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.73-1.04] for <or=4 drinks per day, 0.76 (95% CI 0.59-0.99) for >4 to <or=8 drinks per day and 0.70 (95% CI 0.50-0.97) for >8 drinks per day of alcoholic beverages, with a significant inverse trend in risk (P value = 0.01).

gender.excerpt: Results were consistent in men and women

validated_results.title: Macronutrients, fatty acids, cholesterol and renal cell cancer risk.
validated_results.reason: Italian case-control study reporting an adjusted odds ratio for dietary linoleic acid intake and incident, histologically confirmed renal cell carcinoma.

extraction.comparison_type: highest versus lowest quintile of intake
extraction.population: Hospital-based patients with incident histologically confirmed RCC and controls admitted for acute, nonneoplastic conditions

sample_size.excerpt: Cases were 767 patients with incident, histologically confirmed RCC, admitted to major teaching and general hospitals of the study areas. Controls were 1,534 subjects admitted for acute, nonneoplastic conditions to the same hospitals.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 767 + 1534 = 2301

cases.excerpt: Cases were 767 patients with incident, histologically confirmed RCC, admitted to major teaching and general hospitals of the study areas.

effect_size.excerpt: A direct association with RCC was found for starch intake (OR = 1.9 for highest versus lowest quintile of intake; 95% CI: 1.4-2.6, p-value for trend = 0.001), while an inverse association was found for fats from vegetable sources (OR = 0.6; 95% CI: 0.5-0.8; p-value for trend = 0.002), unsaturated fatty acids (OR = 0.5; 95% CI: 0.4-0.7; p-value for trend = 0.0002), and polyunsaturated fatty acids (OR = 0.5; 95% CI: 0.4-0.7; p-value for trend = 0.001).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Among polyunsaturated fatty acids, linoleic acid (OR = 0.5; 95% CI: 0.4-0.7; p-value for trend = 0.0001) and linolenic acid (OR = 0.7; 95% CI: 0.5-1.0; p-value for trend = 0.01) were inversely related to RCC.
